frameworks.name: Blame-Control Inversion
frameworks.definition: What you blame external forces for is what you give them power over; shifting from blame to self-accountability transfers control to yourself.

frameworks.name: Excuses as Power Transfer
frameworks.definition: Using an excuse ("I can't do X because of Y") makes Y the entity controlling your life outcomes.

claims.text: Whatever you blame external forces for is what also you direct your power towards. When Alex Hormozi blamed his mother for his inability to commit in relationships ("my mother controls my love life"), he relinquished his own agency in that domain; by naming her as the problem, he made her the controller of his romantic outcomes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Blame-pointing is power-pointing: naming an external cause for a negative outcome makes that cause the entity with control over your life in that domain.

claims.text: Every excuse in the form "I can't do X because of Y" makes Y the entity with power over your life. If you say "I can't be successful because of my mother's parenting," you have declared that your mother controls your success.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Self-inflicted suffering as punishment (hurting yourself to hurt a parent who hurt you) causes greater damage to yourself than it causes to the parent; at some point, prolonging the suffering to maintain the control dynamic is your choice, not theirs.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: A person may unconsciously avoid success to avoid validating how they were parented; if they become successful, they fear it implies their upbringing (though harmful) was justified or necessary. This conflict—between not wanting the parent to "win" through the child's success and the desire to actually succeed—can lock a person in underperformance as long as they maintain the emotional tie to the parent's control.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: person equates success with validating the harmful parenting
claims.mechanism: The person unconsciously believes that success = validation of the parent's methods; success therefore feels like betraying themselves or accepting the parent's right to have harmed them; staying unsuccessful becomes the (subconscious) bargain to keep the parent from 'winning.'
bounded_by: Does not apply to people without parental trauma
Does not apply when the person has consciously resolved the parental narrative

claims.text: The moment you choose to take responsibility for your results—decoupling your outcomes from the external "reasons" you have for not succeeding—is the moment you divorce yourself from control by external forces and claim control over yourself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Growth through acceptance of past harm: acknowledging that difficult childhood experiences happened and then consciously choosing "I care [about myself], so I will act in my own interest regardless" shifts the person from victim-blaming narratives to agent-driven action.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Children lack adult skills to process harmful experiences, which means tough parenting circumstances are not a reflection of the child's ability or worth; the adult recognizing this can separate the experience (which happened) from the identity (which they get to choose).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: There is an exact 10-stage scaling roadmap from zero to $100M+ revenue; fewer than 1% of companies complete it. Alex Hormozi has executed it multiple times across software, physical products, service businesses, and brick-and-mortar operations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

anchors.value: complete fewer than all 10 stages (>99% do not finish)

claims.text: The 10-stage roadmap to $100M+ breaks down each stage by 8 business functions, describes the constraint and its symptoms when passing through that stage, and documents the specific steps taken to graduate to the next stage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: Alex Hormozi held a belief in childhood that he would never sustain a long-term committed relationship because his mother had hurt him early in life ("I didn't get enough hugs"). He recognized that by repeatedly saying "my mother is the reason I can't trust people" and "my mother is the reason I can't love anybody," he was giving her complete control over his romantic life. He actively shifted his mindset to "maybe all these things happened, maybe they didn't. Also, who cares? Me. I care. I'm the one who's affected." This reframing moved him from seeing his mother as the controller of his love life to taking responsibility for his own relational choices.

A child experiencing tough parenting (abuse, neglect, or emotional harm) lacks the cognitive and emotional tools an adult has to contextualize and process the experience. At the time, the child may internalize the experience as their own fault or as a reflection of their worth. As an adult, the person can separate the event (which was real and harmful) from the identity they construct (which they can choose), recognizing that the childhood circumstance does not determine adult capability.

practices.text: When you notice yourself using an excuse ("I can't succeed because of X"), pause and recognize that you have just given X power over your life. Consciously choose to take responsibility for your outcome instead.

If you are carrying unresolved parental or childhood trauma, explicitly ask yourself: "Am I staying unsuccessful to punish my parent, or to avoid validating how they parented me?" If yes, recognize that you are choosing your parent's control over your own growth.
